basics.name: Online woodworking joint references: Wikipedia 'Joinery' article (the target of the 'Woodworking joints' redirect) with its per-joint articles and Category:Joinery, WOOD Magazine's joinery hub and joint torture tests, and Fine Woodworking's Joinery project guide and Joinery Shootout strength test
basics.url: Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joinery (the page 'Woodworking joints' redirects here, checked with the MediaWiki API) and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category:Joinery . WOOD Magazine joinery hub: https://www.woodmagazine.com/woodworking-how-to/joinery (live site returned HTTP 402 to automated requests; read via Wayback copy https://web.archive.org/web/20260512002830/https://www.woodmagazine.com/woodworking-how-to/joinery ); door and drawer joint torture test read via https://web.archive.org/web/20241219083706/https://www.woodmagazine.com/woodworking-how-to/doors-drawers/wood-joint-torture-test-2-doors-drawers . Fine Woodworking: https://www.finewoodworking.com/project-guides/joinery and https://www.finewoodworking.com/2009/01/01/joinery-shootout
basics.resource_type: encyclopedia/wiki (Wikipedia) + magazine web guides (WOOD Magazine, Fine Woodworking) with how-to articles, videos and strength tests
basics.cost: Wikipedia: free. WOOD Magazine: free to read online (ad-supported; print magazine and plans are paid). Fine Woodworking: landing pages and previews free; full articles, videos and archive need Fine Woodworking UNLIMITED membership ('less than $10 a month', about USD 99 per year [uncertain])
basics.license: Wikipedia text: Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 (page footer), so text can be reused with attribution and share-alike. WOOD Magazine (Dotdash Meredith / People Inc.) and Fine Woodworking (Taunton Press): all rights reserved; link only, do not copy text or images
basics.language: English (Wikipedia also has joinery articles in many other languages via interlanguage links [uncertain])
basics.year: Wikipedia Joinery article: long-standing article, last edited 23 September 2026 (checked); Mortise and tenon article last edited 15 May 2026. WOOD Magazine: online articles mostly re-posted 2019 from print issues (torture test 2 and pin-and-crescent pages dated 2019), hub still live in 2026; the first joint torture test was in print issue #173 (November 2006) per forum reports [uncertain]. Fine Woodworking: magazine since 1975; Joinery Shootout in issue #203 (January/February 2009); Joinery project guide updated into 2026; bed-bolt alternative article 30 September 2024 (issue #282)
basics.access_barrier: Wikipedia: none. WOOD Magazine: none for readers (but it blocks automated fetching). Fine Woodworking: paywall (membership) for most full articles and videos; free forum and previews
basics.image_license: Wikipedia images are hosted on Wikimedia Commons, mostly CC BY-SA or public domain (per-file licences; e.g. Commons 'Category:Woodworking joints' holds about 280 files in 17 subcategories). WOOD Magazine and Fine Woodworking photos, drawings and videos: all rights reserved
basics.authority_level: Wikipedia: community/unvetted (the Joinery article carries a 'lacks in-text citations' maintenance tag since February 2008). WOOD Magazine and Fine Woodworking: educator/professional (magazine editors and professional furniture makers; the strength tests were done in university or lab test rigs, e.g. WOOD's at Iowa State University)

coverage.covers: Western wood joints for furniture, cabinets and some timber framing. Wikipedia Joinery article: two illustrated tables, 'Traditional' (15 joints: butt, lap, bridle, mortise and tenon, dowel, cross dowel, mitre, box, dovetail, dado/housing, groove, tongue and groove, birdsmouth, cross lap, splice, scarf, Knapp) and 'Modern' (4: pocket-hole, biscuit, floating tenon, stitch and glue), plus sections on wood strength and movement, reinforcing, and terms (cheek, shoulder). Category:Joinery has 38 articles (incl. butterfly joint, Edmund key, Ortman key, Phoenician joint, Nuki, mason's miter, joggle, toenailing, spline) and 5 subcategories; per-joint articles such as Mortise and tenon list about 15 named variants. WOOD Magazine hub: about 60 linked how-to articles (box joints, biscuits, dovetails, frame-and-panel, half-laps, miters, mortise and tenon, pocket screws, drawbore, sliding dovetail, threading wood, kerf bending, pin-and-crescent, breadboard ends, splines, MDF and plywood joints) plus two joint torture tests. Fine Woodworking Joinery guide: 5 chapters (rabbets and dadoes; mortise-and-tenon; dovetails; box/finger joints; joints with fasteners: dowels, biscuits, Dominos, pocket screws) plus hundreds of member articles and videos, including knock-down joinery (bed bolts, slip tenons with hidden bolts)
coverage.organisation: Wikipedia: a table per era (traditional vs modern), each row joint name + small picture + one-paragraph plain description, and each name links to its own article; plus an alphabetical category. Easy to scan by picture, but no grouping by job. WOOD Magazine: a topic hub page of article cards ordered by recency/popularity, with top tags by joint family (box joints, biscuits, dovetails, frame-and-panel, half-laps, miters, mortise and tenon, pocket screws); good for 'how to cut X' but you need to know the name. Fine Woodworking: project guide in 5 family chapters, each a curated list of articles; plus site search and forum
coverage.scope_match: medium. Woodworking joinery is an in-scope family (lowest priority by making method). These sites are the most linkable, current and illustrated web sources for wood joint TYPES, and include clever ones (sliding dovetail, drawbore, tusk and wedged tenons, pin-and-crescent / Knapp joint, cross dowel, bed bolts and knock-down joints, Edmund and Ortman keys). But they are wood-only, and most joints are permanent glued joints rather than the project's special behaviours
coverage.taxonomy_used: Wikipedia: traditional vs modern (2 top-level groups) in the article, plus Wikipedia's category tree (Category:Joinery with 5 subcategories; related Category:Timber framing, Category:Woodworking). WOOD Magazine: by joint family tags (about 8 top-level tags). Fine Woodworking: by joint family (5 chapters: rabbets and dadoes, mortise-and-tenon, dovetails, box/finger joints, joints with fasteners)
coverage.example_types: Sliding dovetail (WOOD 'The Never-Fail Sliding Dovetail'; Fine Woodworking dovetail chapter); drawbored mortise and tenon (a peg through offset holes pulls the joint tight; WOOD and FWW); tusk tenon (through tenon locked by a removable wedge, knock-down; Wikipedia Mortise and tenon); wedged half-dovetail mortise (Wikipedia); hammer-headed tenon (Wikipedia); pegged/pinned tenon; loose (floating) tenon and Domino; pin-and-crescent / Knapp joint (machine-made Victorian drawer joint, 1871; WOOD and Wikipedia); cross dowel (threaded metal barrel nut pulled tight by a bolt; Wikipedia); bed bolts and slip-tenon hidden-bolt knock-down bed joint (FWW 2010 and 2024); butterfly joint (bow-tie key); Edmund key and Ortman key (Wikipedia category); Phoenician joint (Wikipedia category); birdsmouth joint; scarf joint; bridle joint; lock-rabbet and lock-miter drawer joints (WOOD torture test); cope-and-stick; splined miter; pocket-hole joint; stitch and glue
coverage.making_methods: Woodwork (hand tools, router, tablesaw, biscuit and Domino joiners, pocket-hole jigs), some timber framing and boat building (stitch and glue). WOOD also covers MDF and plywood joints. No 3D printing; little CNC
coverage.item_count: Wikipedia: 19 joints in the Joinery article tables; 38 articles in Category:Joinery; about 280 files in Commons 'Category:Woodworking joints'. WOOD Magazine joinery hub: about 60 articles. Fine Woodworking: joinery guide in 5 chapters linking dozens of articles; site-wide 1,900+ member articles and 900+ technique videos (members page)
coverage.special_behaviours_covered: Knock-down / hand-release (tusk tenons, bed bolts, cross dowels, slip-tenon bolted bed joints) and self-locking by shape or wedging (sliding dovetails, dovetails, wedged and drawbored tenons, keys). Adhesives: WOOD has 'How To Choose and Use the Right Glue' and edge-gluing articles, and the torture tests used yellow (PVA) glue; Wikipedia has Category:Woodworking adhesives (6 articles) and a 'Materials used for joining' section. Not covered: torque-limiting, ratchet, detent, over-centre, compliant, print-in-place, gear trains, powered connectors
coverage.entry_structure: Wikipedia: joint name, thumbnail image, one-paragraph description in the table; linked article with etymology/history, description, types/variants, gallery, references. WOOD: magazine-style how-to with step photos, drawings, sometimes video, tool setup, tips. Fine Woodworking: long-form how-to by a named maker with photos, drawings and often video (members only). The torture-test articles add measured strength results and charts
coverage.audience_level: Hobbyist (WOOD Magazine, Wikipedia) to serious hobbyist and professional furniture maker (Fine Woodworking)

usefulness.beginner_friendliness: Wikipedia: medium to high (plain one-line descriptions with a picture for each joint, but thin and patchily cited). WOOD Magazine: high (practical, shop-tested, lots of photos, 'lessons' in plain words). Fine Woodworking: medium (excellent quality but aimed at skilled woodworkers, and paywalled)
usefulness.has_images: yes. Wikipedia: simple diagrams and photos (often SVG line drawings, some GIFs). WOOD and Fine Woodworking: high-quality step photos and technical drawings
usefulness.has_animations: Wikipedia: a few animated GIFs (e.g. Pocket-hole joint being assembled, dowel and groove joint GIFs). WOOD Magazine: embedded videos (e.g. 'Watch us smash our way through door and drawer joints' torture-test video). Fine Woodworking: many member-only videos and a short video on the Joinery Shootout test method
usefulness.gaps: No selector by job or by behaviour (no 'I need it to come apart' or 'I need to join end to end' entry point), except scattered advice in the strength tests. Wikipedia's list is short (19 joints) and misses many clever joints that do have articles; its category is flat and alphabetical. WOOD and FWW need the joint name to search, and FWW is paywalled. None cover 3D-printed, CNC or laser-cut adaptations of these joints
usefulness.good_for_entry_links: Wikipedia: yes, very good; stable per-joint URLs such as https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mortise_and_tenon , plus Commons images that can be reused under their licences. WOOD Magazine: yes, per-article URLs (e.g. https://www.woodmagazine.com/woodworking-how-to/joinery/pin-and-crescent-joint ), though old URLs have moved before (older /woodworking-tips/techniques/joinery/... links show up on archived pages) and the site blocks bots. Fine Woodworking: stable dated URLs (e.g. https://www.finewoodworking.com/2024/09/30/a-clever-alternative-to-bed-bolts ) but readers hit a paywall
usefulness.reusable_data: Wikipedia: structured and reusable: MediaWiki API, category tree, Wikidata items, CC BY-SA 4.0 text and per-file Commons licences; the joint list can be built on with attribution and share-alike. WOOD and Fine Woodworking: scrape-only in principle, but all rights reserved and WOOD blocks automated access, so not reusable beyond linking and citing
usefulness.maintained: All three are live and maintained in 2026: Wikipedia Joinery edited 23 Sep 2026; WOOD Magazine hub live (Wayback copy May 2026, live page answers but blocks bots); Fine Woodworking guide updated into 2026. Wayback copies exist for the WOOD pages
usefulness.ideas_to_borrow: (1) Wikipedia's table: name + small picture + one-sentence plain description, with aliases in the description (e.g. bridle joint 'also known as open tenon, open mortise and tenon, or tongue and fork'), which is exactly the encyclopedia's row format. (2) Split old vs modern (traditional vs machine or jig-based) as a secondary filter. (3) WOOD's torture tests: present results as 'FINDING' and 'LESSON' pairs and a ranked chart, and give a plain 'choose this for...' conclusion (e.g. half-laps for frames holding glass or mirrors). (4) Separate tests by load type (pull-apart vs shear/racking), with an everyday picture of each load ('a child hanging from an open cabinet door'). (5) FWW's 'joints with fasteners' chapter as a bridge between pure joinery and hardware
usefulness.design_rules_given: Yes, some numbers. WOOD torture test 2 (door and drawer joints, red oak and poplar, yellow glue, Iowa State University rig): average drawer joint held 1,489 lb pull-apart but only 80 lb shear; average door joint 1,214 lb pull-apart and 511 lb shear; half-lap withstood more than twice the shear force of the next strongest door joint; tenons one-third of stock thickness were strong enough. Fine Woodworking Joinery Shootout (#203, 18 joint types, 5 samples each, cherry 3/4 x 2 1/2 x 8 in.): half-lap strongest and stub tenon weakest (opened page); forum-reported figures include 1/4 in. M&T 717 lb, 3/8 in. M&T about 1,475 lb, pocket screws 698 lb (Sawmill Creek, from the magazine) and half-lap 1,603 lb, bridle 1,560 lb, Domino 597 lb, biscuit 545 lb (search summaries of forum posts) [uncertain]. FWW 'The Mighty Wedge' gives about 5 degrees as a wedge angle (search summary only) [uncertain]
usefulness.file_formats: Web pages (HTML), images (SVG, PNG, JPG, GIF on Commons), video (WOOD and FWW), PDF downloads of FWW articles for members, SketchUp plans for FWW members
usefulness.terminology_value: good. Wikipedia gives aliases for many joints (e.g. dado = housing joint = trench joint; Knapp joint = pin-and-scallop = pin-and-cove = scallop-and-dowel) and interlanguage links for translations; WOOD adds US shop names (e.g. pin-and-crescent)
usefulness.decision_support: Limited. No flow chart or filter on any of the three. WOOD's torture tests give ranked comparison charts and 'choose this for...' conclusions; FWW's Joinery Shootout gives a ranked strength comparison of 18 frame joints; Wikipedia gives none beyond one-line descriptions. The FWW guide notes the method depends on the situation but gives no selection chart
usefulness.derived_from_or_overlaps: Wikipedia's Joinery article cites WOOD Magazine's 'Wood Joint Torture Test' and Fine Woodworking's history of the cove-and-pin joint, and older content from sawdustmaking.com (archived). Fine Woodworking is the Taunton Press magazine, so it overlaps with Taunton books such as Rogowski's Complete Illustrated Guide to Joinery (Rogowski also writes for FWW). All three overlap with Noll's The Joint Book and with commercial guides (Kreg, WoodWorkers Guild of America, Popular Woodworking, Family Handyman) that repeat the same core list
